Our class sends a thank-you letter to a visitor who showed us how to care for books. Each pupil writes one sentence, and two helpers arrange the sentences on a clean page. We put the finished letter into an envelope and check the address before posting it. A week later, a reply says that our visitor is absolutely delighted to hear what we learned. The class reads the reply together and notices that specific examples made our thanks clear. We keep a copy of both letters in our class record, with the real dates they were sent.

The school craft group is making a large picture with pieces of coloured paper. Before the work begins, a helper gives each pupil a glove with separate parts for the fingers. The teacher explains that this activity uses a messy paste and shows how to keep the table covered. The group decides to add a paper tree near the edge so that the picture looks more complete. They check the space before putting on the paste, rather than moving sticky pieces many times. When they finish, they remove the covers and leave the work area as tidy as they found it.
The cushion changes shape easily when I press it. It does not feel hard against my hand.
Lin peels a small picture from its backing and presses it onto her notebook. Its sticky back holds it there.
The two bags are similar, but one is bigger.
这两个包很相像，但其中一个更大。
I put a coin into the machine.
我把一枚硬币投入机器。
This pillow is soft and comfortable.
Mia puts a star sticker on her notebook.
米娅在笔记本上贴了一张星形贴纸。
Leaving the tap running is a waste of water.
让水龙头一直开着是浪费水。
There are five items in my shopping basket.
我的购物篮里有五件商品。

Sam missed the first part of a group lesson about folding paper boxes. He asks Ella to explain the first fold before he tries to copy the finished box. She takes a fresh sheet and shows him how two edges meet in the middle. One bit of the paper is torn, so they turn the sheet and choose a different edge. Sam repeats the step slowly and tells Ella what he is doing. When the fold is ready, he can continue with the group instead of guessing from the final shape.

A wooden name board is loose outside the school garden. The pupils leave it on the ground and ask the caretaker to look at it. He finds a bent nail that no longer holds the board firmly in place. A single new nail is enough for this small repair, but he checks the wood before using it. The pupils watch from a safe distance and draw the repair in their garden notebook. After the board is fixed, they check that visitors can read the plant names clearly again.
The shop sells chocolate in long rectangular pieces. Mia buys one of these pieces and breaks off a small square.
Our lunch set contains soup, rice and fruit. The fruit is part of the set, not an extra order.
The result of the heavy rain is a wet playground.
大雨的结果是操场湿了。
Put the empty chocolate wrapper in the bin.
把空的巧克力包装纸放进垃圾桶。
Mia buys a bar of chocolate.
The cloth has a pattern of stars.

Our class prepares materials for a small model of the neighbourhood. Cutting large sheets before planning the shapes could be a waste of paper. Each item on our supply list is checked against the materials already in the cupboard. A pupil finds several useful pieces left from an earlier project. We draw the shapes on these pieces first and only take new sheets when necessary. At the end, we save the unused pieces in a labelled box so the next group can find them easily.

The drama group borrows several animal toys for a classroom performance. One toy rabbit has soft fabric, and its owner asks the group to keep it away from wet paint. A helper puts a sticker with the owner’s name on the rabbit’s storage box. The pupils make a separate clean corner for all the borrowed toys. After the performance, they use the names on the boxes to return each toy to the right person. The rabbit goes home clean and dry, and the owner thanks them for taking care of it.
The sweet smell can attract bees to the flowers.

Our nature group finds a small object beside a leaf on the garden path. At first it looks like a piece of bark, so we leave it where it is and look closely. Then it moves, and we notice six thin legs beneath its body. The teacher helps us recognise it as an insect rather than a piece of wood. An ant crosses the path. We count its six legs and watch it walk towards a crack in the ground.

We are getting the school hall ready for a puppet show. The sun is bright at first, so we can see the stage clearly. As it grows later, the sun seems to go down behind the trees. Ben cannot see the lost dog from here. Lily tells him about its small size, brown ears and long white tail.
At first, Mia makes many mistakes in her handwriting. She practises carefully each day, and after a month her writing is much clearer.

The bicycle club plans to lend bikes to visitors on Sunday. Before anyone rides, the teacher checks what might go wrong with each bike. The club reads the price notice and decides which repairs are necessary now. They spend their small budget on safe brakes before buying colourful flags. On Sunday, visitors receive checked bikes and clear instructions for a safe ride.

Grandma invites us to spend the evening in her garden. We sit beside the pond and watch the water become still. The water level can go down when Grandma uses some to water her pots. Tonight she only needs a small can, so she takes very little. Later, the garden lamps go out because their timer reaches its set time. We use a torch to follow Grandma back along the stone path. Inside, she gives us warm milk and asks what we enjoyed about the evening.

By the next evening, the bear still misses home but feels less alone.

Our class builds paper hot-air balloons for a story display. The balloons hang from strings above a painted mountain scene. In our story, one balloon can rise into the clear morning sky. We hear about a free puppet show from our school noticeboard. It is in the library, and the first performance begins after lunch. Lily wants a seat near the front so she can see the small puppets. When we finish eating, she asks us to hurry up. We put away our lunch boxes promptly and walk to the library together. There are still several empty seats near the stage when we arrive. We sit down quietly and wait for the storyteller to open the curtain.

I telephone the library to ask about a book for our project. The librarian asks me to hold on while she checks the shelf. I keep the phone beside my ear and wait quietly. She returns and says the book is missing from its usual place. She checks the returns desk and finds it under another large book. In the end, she says I can collect it that afternoon. I thank her for looking carefully and tell my group that our plan can continue.
The bank is next to the library, with no other building between them.
This jacket usually costs sixty dollars. Today the shop offers a special price of forty dollars.
The concert starts at seven. Our group reaches the hall before the doors close, and the music begins exactly as scheduled.

By the third try, Ben follows the whole pattern and thanks everyone for waiting.

The owner explains that the bridge is closed, so we choose the lakeside path. After checking the weather, we thank him and write our new plan together.

Our class is carrying empty boxes into the storage room after a fair. I hear my name and turn round before moving any farther. Maya is standing behind me with a loose shoelace trailing on the floor. She puts her box down so that she will not fall down while walking. I hold it steady as she ties the lace and checks the other shoe. Then we make sure the doorway is clear before lifting both boxes again. The work takes a little longer, but we finish without a dropped box or an injury.

On Sunday mornings, our neighbours take exercise together beside the river. One morning, they stop when they hear a small dog barking below the path. Its lead is caught on a low branch near the fast water. The dog is in danger, and nobody wants to make it jump towards the river. The group stays back while one neighbour calls a trained rescue worker. The worker frees the lead and brings the frightened dog onto the path. Soon its owner arrives, thanks everyone and takes it home on a shorter lead.
Please slow down when you drive near the school.
Ada keeps reading long after everyone else falls asleep. At midnight her lamp is still on and she is still awake.
Before speaking on stage, Jin slowly draws a large amount of air into his lungs. Then he lets it out and begins his first sentence.
Ben's father does not need to lose weight, according to his doctor.
按医生的说法，本的爸爸不需要减肥。

We stay up to watch the final match.

At the craft club, I set a small wooden chair on the workbench. The teacher asks me to turn it round so its back faces the window. Now the light shows a crack that I could not see before. We repair it together and leave the chair for the glue to dry. A label tells everyone to keep away from the workbench until tomorrow. Other members choose a different table and continue making their small shelves. When we return the next day, the chair is firm and ready for painting.

A new walking group meets outside our neighbourhood centre every Saturday. The members want to keep fit and enjoy spending time outdoors together. Today they choose a short route through a quiet park near the centre. “Look out!” says the leader when a child on a scooter approaches the group. Everyone steps calmly to one side and gives the child room to pass. Later, they sit on a bench and compare ideas for next week's walk. They choose another easy route so that new members can join without feeling rushed.
The library faces the park. It is across from the park.
For the festival, flags hang in every street. They cover the whole town rather than just the main square.
After a long train journey, the group finally steps onto the platform at their destination station. Their journey to that station is complete.
The town is famous for its beautiful gardens.
这个镇因美丽的花园而闻名。

At the school concert, Noor carries a small drum onto the stage. “Take care on the last step,” the teacher says, moving a cable aside. Noor reaches her chair safely but notices that her hands are shaking. She takes a deep breath before lifting the sticks into position. Her partner gives a quiet signal, and they begin the rhythm together. After the first few beats, Noor remembers the pattern they practised all week. The piece ends smoothly, and she leaves the stage smiling beside her partner.

Uncle Ben tells us about his new walking class. After a check-up, he and his doctor agreed on a plan to lose weight. He says his class begins gently, with time to warm up before the longer walk. The teacher also asks members to choose a pace that suits their own plan. Ben enjoys the company of the other adults more than he expected. He keeps a notebook about how he feels, rather than comparing himself with everyone. When he visits us, his favourite stories are about the people and places he meets.
These two villages are famous for their tea. People come from far away to buy it.
Chen cannot untie a tight knot in a rope. His grandmother shows him each step, and he finally loosens it by following her guidance.
The café cannot serve our meal yet. We stay at the table and talk until the food is brought out.

Our class takes a bus to a small local history centre. We arrive at the centre early, before its front doors open. The teacher shows us a bakery across from the entrance on the opposite side of the road. Its owner shows old photographs of the street in the window. While we wait, we compare the pictures with the buildings around us. A tall wall in one photograph no longer stands, but the little bridge remains. By opening time, we already have questions about changes in the neighbourhood.

Our town holds a weekend exhibition of handmade animal models. At the entrance, a large paper fox stands between a tree and a painted rock. Children follow its footprints to a room full of smaller creatures. There are models from families all over the town, not just from one school. Every display has a card explaining how its maker reused ordinary materials. My favourite bird has wings made from a broken umbrella. Before leaving, we write down ideas for things we could make from objects at home.
The soup is cold. Please warm it up before lunch.
It is past midnight, but Ben is still reading at his desk. He does not go to bed until two in the morning.
Mia is riding too fast near the gate. She gently uses the brakes so that her bicycle moves at a safer speed.

Our class is building a display of small wooden houses for the school fair. Ben puts one house near the edge, where it could fall off the table. “Take care!” Mia says, pointing to the space beneath it. They move the house towards the middle and place a wide board underneath. Then they test the display with a gentle push before inviting younger visitors over. By checking the position first, the two pupils keep their work safe without stopping the fair.

Ben and his father plan a gentle walk around the lake on Sunday. His father wants to lose weight under his doctor's guidance, so they choose an easy route. Before starting, Ben needs to take a deep breath to calm his excitement. They agree that the aim is to enjoy moving together rather than race. At each bench, they stop briefly to look at the water and talk. When they return, both want another walk, and Ben adds it to their family calendar.
The taxi door is open. Please get in and sit down.
The pupils leave the marked path and cannot find their campsite. None of them recognises the trees around them.
The bus stops outside the museum. Ben steps from it onto the pavement and waits for his classmates.
We get back to school before lunch.
我们在午饭前返回学校。

The train gets in at eight.
The farmers get the rice in before the rain.

Take a map so you do not get lost.

Our gardening group notices that young plants bend when strong wind crosses the playground. We want to protect them without keeping the whole bed indoors. A local gardener agrees to provide some wooden supports for our experiment. We place the supports beside the plants and tie the stems loosely with soft string. Each afternoon, two pupils check that the string is not hurting the growing stems. After a windy week, we compare our notes and discuss which support worked best.

Our map club is choosing a place for an imaginary walking camp. The first map shows a high hill, but the path to it is very steep. The second shows a quiet valley only twenty metres above sea level. What's more, its marked route has several sheltered places where our group could rest safely. We compare the distances and explain why the second place suits beginners better. Although the camp exists only on paper, the discussion teaches us to use several map details together.
Use the bridge to go across the river from one side to the other.
A dog is sleeping near the gate. The visitor leaves that area so it can rest without being disturbed.
Mia reaches the library but realises her card is at home. She returns home to collect it.
We get to school before eight.
We go across the bridge to reach the island.

Our class must take a box of books to the community reading room. The teacher checks a map so that we can get there before the afternoon activity begins. At the door, Mia remembers a pen she left behind on her last visit. She asks the worker politely and is pleased to get her pen back from the lost-property drawer. Then everyone carries a few books to the low shelves and checks their labels. We finish in time and stay to hear younger children choose their first story.

Our school radio team is waiting for a visiting group from another town. Their train will get in at ten, so we have time to practise our welcome. Ben asks how the recording project is getting on while we wait. Mia says the opening music is ready, but two speakers still need a quiet place to record. We offer the empty music room and carry a microphone there before the visitors arrive. The waiting time becomes useful because one question helps us notice and solve a small problem.
The clock is on your left. Look left to see it.
At the crossing, Ben turns his eyes towards the road on his right. He checks for bicycles before taking a step.
The walking group takes an unfamiliar path. Soon they cannot identify the route back to their campsite.

I look around to find my friend in the crowd.
我环顾四周，在人群中寻找朋友。
We look around the museum before lunch.

Look left to see the clock beside the door.
Look right to see the picture beside the window.
We lose our way when we walk without a map.

I meet Ben on my way to school.
Mia sees a rainbow on her way home.
米娅在回家路上看见彩虹。
We plan to visit the museum tomorrow.
我们计划明天参观博物馆。

Our art group arrives at the park gate with paper and coloured pencils. Before we get to the pond, Ben discovers that his sketchbook is missing. He wants to go back to the gate, where he last remembers holding it. The teacher stays with him while the others wait on a bench in sight. They find the book beside the noticeboard and check that none of the pages is wet. When they rejoin us, Ben draws the noticeboard as a reminder to check his bag before moving.

Our class plans to go on a trip to a farm after studying how vegetables grow. We will leave for the farm after morning registration, so everyone brings a packed lunch. The farmer sends a list of questions that visitors can investigate during the day. Mia chooses to compare the leaves of two plants instead of trying to see everything. She draws a simple table in her notebook with room for pictures and observations. Preparing one clear question helps her look forward to the visit and know what to notice.
The cars hardly move. There is a traffic jam on the road.

Our class is practising road observation in a model street on the playground. The teacher asks each pupil to look left, then look right, and keep checking before crossing. Ben notices a bicycle hidden partly behind a tall cardboard box. He waits until he can see the whole route instead of copying the pupil ahead. Afterwards, our group moves the box and discusses how objects can block a clear view. The exercise reminds us that knowing a routine matters less if we stop watching the actual road.

Mia and her aunt are on their way to the library with a bag of donated books. They try a new lane because the usual street is closed for repairs. At a fork, they realise they could lose their way if they keep guessing. Instead, they stop by a shop and compare the street sign with the aunt's map. A worker confirms that the library is just beyond the next corner, beside the park. They arrive only a little late and explain the useful route check to the librarian.
The soup is a little bit hot, so wait a moment before eating it.

The visitors' bus is delayed by a traffic jam on the main road outside town. Rows of cars are hardly moving, so the driver checks an alternative route before changing direction. At the next junction, the map tells him to turn right towards the river bridge. A helper phones our school to explain the delay and give a new arrival time. We move the welcome game indoors and keep the first activity short enough for the visitors. Good information lets both groups adjust calmly instead of worrying about an unexplained absence.

At the village airport, our group watches a small plane prepare for its first flight of the day. A few pupils sketch its wings while the others note questions for the guide. We stay behind the marked line until the plane can take off safely. As it rises, Ben notices that his drawing shows the wheels but misses part of one wing. The guide lets us compare photographs afterwards instead of moving closer to the runway. We complete our notes and learn that careful viewing can continue without crossing a safety boundary.
The shop sells three kinds of bread: brown, white and fruit bread.
At the craft table, pupils can choose paper, cloth, wood and clay. The materials come in many different types.
The swimmers reach the far end of the pool. The coach asks them to return to the starting end for the next exercise.

Our class makes a sound map of the streets near the school library. At the gate, the teacher asks us to turn right into a quieter lane. Each group gets a piece of paper to mark places where different sounds can be heard. We record footsteps, birds and a shop bell, but do not write down private conversations. Back inside, we compare the maps and notice that the same corner sounds different at different times. The project helps us listen closely to familiar places and respect the people who use them.

Our school starts a repair table for pupils who want to fix simple items rather than throw them away. Mia brings a pair of gloves with one small hole near the thumb. There is a lot of useful cloth in the donation box, so she chooses a matching patch. An adult helper shows her how to hold the material safely before she begins. Ben draws the steps on a card so the next visitor can follow the same process. By the end of lunch, the gloves are useful again and our table has its first instruction card.
This short story is a piece of writing by a young student.
The shop sells shoes as two matching items, one for each foot. Ben buys one complete set.
Rain falls heavily for several hours. By evening, there is a very large amount of water in the empty bucket.

Our drama group is showing visitors how to use the new changing area behind the stage. From the hall door, they turn left at the noticeboard and follow the blue arrows. Inside, each performer can take off an outdoor coat and hang it on a numbered hook. Mia tests the instructions with a younger pupil on his first visit to the room. He finds the door easily but cannot see the numbers hidden behind some hanging scarves. We move the labels above the hooks, making the whole route clearer for the next show.

A few pupils volunteer to check the supplies before our class cleans the community garden. Each team will receive gloves, a rubbish bag and a bottle of water for the afternoon. Ben compares the list with the boxes and finds that one team has no gloves. Rather than starting that team early, he asks an adult helper to bring another set. While they wait, Mia explains which garden paths must stay clear for other visitors. The short supply check prevents confusion and helps everyone begin with the equipment they need.
Both Mia and Ben enjoy the game; neither of the two children wants to stop.
The teacher says pupils can reuse many household items. She then mentions one old jar that could hold pencils.
The reading challenge lasts twenty minutes. Ben finishes after eighteen minutes, before the full limit is reached.
My bag is different from yours in colour.
我的包和你的包颜色不同。
Both Mia and Ben enjoy reading.
The story is both funny and exciting.
这个故事既有趣又令人兴奋。

有些动物白天睡觉，例如许多蝙蝠就是这样。
The journey takes less than an hour.
More and more students use the new reading room.

“May I borrow your ruler?” “Of course. Here you are.”

“Do you mind if I sit here?” “Of course not. Please sit down.”

Our class visits a museum with two entrances, and we agree to meet at the one beside the garden. The route note says to turn left after the fountain instead of following the crowd towards the shop. Ben thinks that checking the note is a waste of time because the building is easy to see. However, Mia points out that seeing the building does not tell them which entrance to use. They read the final line together and reach the garden gate before the rest of their group. Ben keeps the note for the return journey, realising that a short check can prevent a long detour.

At our class picnic, Mia chooses a soft drink without alcohol from the refreshments table. It is plain sparkling water, and she wants to add a slice of orange to it for flavour. Before doing so, she checks that the knife and fruit belong to the shared preparation area. An adult helps cut the orange while Mia puts the used plate in the washing tray. Other pupils choose plain water or fruit juice, and nobody has to copy another person's choice. Keeping the table tidy makes it easier for everyone to prepare a drink they enjoy.
Quite a few students join the club—thirty-two in all.
The garden has several flowers with bright colours. The notice names roses and sunflowers as two members of this group.
Our display nearly falls because one leg is loose. A helper holds it steady in time, so none of our models breaks.
There is plenty of water for everyone.

“How much do you read?” “Quite a lot.”

Thanks to our teacher, we understand the difficult question.

I agree with your idea about the class trip.

The result agrees with our earlier measurements.
结果与我们先前的测量一致。
I ask the teacher for some paper.

Our school club has less than an hour to prepare a story corner before the visitors arrive. Mia asks whether we should spend most of it making a large new sign. “Of course not,” Ben replies, because the chairs and books are not ready yet. They agree to reuse last month's sign and give each helper one clear job. Ten minutes before opening, everyone checks that the walkway between the chairs stays wide enough. The corner opens calmly because the group chooses necessary work before adding optional decoration.

More and more families are using our school's weekend swap shelf for items they no longer need. Each item needs a short note so that another family knows its condition. For example, a puzzle note can say that all its pieces are present but the box is worn. Mia and Ben compare two notes and notice that clear details are more useful than saying “nice”. They make a small question card asking about missing parts, damage and safe use. The shelf becomes easier to use as families share honest information instead of relying on appearances alone.
The classmates are friendly to the new student and invite him to play.
The class asks Hana to show her drawings. She smiles and says she would happily share them with everyone.
A new pupil drops his books. Mina gently helps him collect them and checks that he is all right.

Our group is choosing a place for a small class display about local plants. I agree with Lina that the bright wall near the door will be easy for visitors to notice. Before using it, we ask the teacher for permission because another group may need the space. She checks the class plan and finds that the wall is free next week. We measure the space and choose only the pictures that will fit without covering the door notice. Our final plan records both the location and the date when we may put up the display.

The community centre invites families to an afternoon of simple indoor games. The helpers prepare games such as matching pictures and building paper towers. Quite a few families arrive early, so the helpers open a second table before the start. Each table has a short instruction card that parents and children can read together. When one game becomes crowded, a helper explains the other choices rather than rushing anyone. By spreading across the tables, the visitors find enough room to enjoy the activities.
I come from Guangzhou; it is my hometown.

Bo cannot find his library card. His friend finds it and calmly tells him that everything is all right.
The nurse cares for sick children.

During a class interview, Mr Li describes how he learned to play the violin. He first joined a music group at the age of nine and practised with a neighbour. Mr Li smiles and says they sometimes meet to play their favourite pieces together.

Our exchange group includes pupils who come from several different towns. At first, we know little about one another beyond the names on our badges. For our first project, two pupils plan a poster while the others gather information for it. When the plans do not fit together, we discuss the problem instead of blaming a new partner. By the final meeting, the badges are less important because we recognise each other’s interests and strengths.

Two pupils are paired for a school project about favourite places. Lena is from a seaside town, while Amir lives near the hills. They get on well with each other, even though their first ideas for the project are quite different. Lena wants to show a harbour, and Amir wants to draw a walking path through trees. They choose a two-part poster with space for both places and a short comparison in the middle. Their teacher praises how the design allows both partners to contribute rather than making one abandon an idea.

Our class would like to interview a former pupil who now designs gardens. We hope to learn how drawing and careful observation help in her work. The teacher offers to give her a call after we prepare a short list of questions. We remove questions that repeat the same point and choose five that connect to our current project. A new member joins our board-game club halfway through the term. We want to be friendly to him, so we introduce ourselves and explain where the games are kept. At the first table, we choose a game whose rules can be explained in a few minutes. This gives everyone a chance to talk and get along with a new partner without a difficult start. Later, he teaches us a different game that he used to play with his cousins. By the end of the meeting, he is both a learner and someone with a useful idea for the club.

Visitors at the school exhibition come from several nearby neighbourhoods. Our class puts a simple map near the entrance to help them find the rooms. One visitor pauses by my desk and says, “Excuse me, where is the room with the garden models?” I point to the room on the map and explain the route using two clear landmarks. She repeats the room number to check her understanding before walking away. Afterwards, I add a larger arrow to the map because several visitors asked the same question.

Instead, she offers a spare sheet and asks whether he would like to draw a place he enjoys. Their drawings start a relaxed conversation, and soon they are planning a picture together.

Our class discusses what it means to create a safe space for practising new skills. Everyone is invited to make a promise about how to treat classmates during practice. We agree not to make fun of someone who needs more time or makes an error. Instead, we can ask whether the person wants a hint, an example or another quiet try. Later, when a pupil struggles with a rhythm, his partner offers to tap it slowly with him. The class sees that the agreement matters most when it changes what people actually do.

When I join the chess club, I want to make friends as well as learn the game. At the first meeting, I sit alone because I am unsure how to join a table. The leader suggests asking one player whether I may watch the end of a game. I decide to take her advice and ask politely instead of waiting for someone to notice me. The player makes room, explains the final moves and invites me to try the next game. By the time the meeting ends, I know two names and have a reason to look forward to returning.

Our group is running late while setting up chairs for a school event. One pupil begins to shout at his partner because a row is in the wrong place. The leader steps in and says, “Take it easy; let us check the plan before moving anything else.” They discover that the two pupils were looking at different versions of the seating plan. The leader gives everyone the current version, and the pupil apologises for raising his voice. Working from the same plan, the group corrects the row and finishes the setup together.

A pupil from another class joins our lunchtime gardening group for the first time. I would like to make friends with her, but I do not yet know what she enjoys doing. While we fill small pots with soil, I talk with her about the plants she sees near her home. She tells me about a climbing plant that covers a wall, and I describe herbs on our balcony. We notice a shared interest in useful plants and choose labels for the herb pots together. When the session ends, we agree to check the new shoots at the next meeting.

During a group project, I accidentally knock a paper model from the table. For a moment I am tempted to tell a lie and say that the wind moved it. Instead, I decide to tell the group about what happened while everyone is still nearby. I explain that my bag caught the model as I turned, and I offer to help repair it. My partners are disappointed, but they appreciate knowing the cause and help collect the fallen pieces. We repair the model and choose a safer place for bags before continuing our work.
We would like to visit the museum this Sunday, if possible.
Our group needs an idea for Sunday. Lily suggests visiting the free art show and asks whether everyone likes that plan.
Ben draws a cloud above his house. Its shape is so much like a rabbit that everyone notices the long ears.

Our family usually visits the park at the weekend. This Saturday, rain keeps us inside, so we choose a different activity. At the moment, Mum is spreading a large map across the table. We are planning a walking route for the next sunny day. My brother marks places where we can stop and rest. I find a short path near a pond that Grandma may enjoy. Even without going outside today, we are making a useful plan together.

Our class is collecting books for a small reading corner. The teacher says we need at least twenty books to get started. On Wednesday, we count twenty-three books from the children's homes. Our first box is full of stories about animals and adventures. We sort them by topic and check that every page is clean. Two children make labels while the others arrange chairs near the shelf. On Friday, the corner opens, and everyone can find something interesting to read.

I ask whether she would like to share her pencils with me. She smiles and gives me a brown one for my own picture. We talk about the animals we like and help put the pencils away. The small conversation makes the next school day feel much easier for both of us.

His sister says it is better to tell the librarian about what really happened. Ben takes the book back and explains his mistake honestly. The librarian thanks him for telling her and shows him how to protect damaged pages. Ben feels relieved and handles borrowed books more carefully after that day.

The quiet walk and a fresh change leave me ready for a comfortable evening.

Grandfather joins an evening language class because he wants to speak with a new neighbour. At first, he often makes mistakes when choosing the endings of words. He can ask about the neighbour's garden and understand a simple reply. Some words still puzzle him, so he writes questions for his next lesson. He says that being understood matters more to him than sounding perfect immediately.

Before a storm, our library group helps prepare the small outdoor book box. I note down the titles of books we move into the main building. Another volunteer checks the box roof for gaps where water could enter. We make sure that the empty box is firmly shut before leaving. The careful record makes the work quick and prevents anyone from searching for missing books.

Our class plans a recorded interview with a clock repairer for the school radio show. Ben can tell time on the large classroom clock, but he wants to understand clocks without numbers. We telephone the repairer during lunch, when she is helping a customer in her shop. She says she will ring us back after the repair is safely finished. While waiting, we choose three clear questions and test the recorder with the teacher. Her later call gives us enough quiet time to discuss how different clock faces show the same information.

Our community art club wants an experienced visitor to give lessons to beginners during the school holiday. Mia offers to ring her up with the club leader beside her to explain the plan. Before calling, they write down the number of learners and the materials already available. The visitor asks whether the room has tables that can be cleaned easily after painting. We check with the caretaker and send a clear answer before agreeing on the first date. Planning the practical details helps the guest decide what she can teach and what equipment she should bring.
We have an interest in growing plants and want to join the gardening club.
One group is painting the sign while another group builds the stand. Both activities are happening together during this lesson.

Our history club visits a workshop where a guide demonstrates an old candle holder. He asks us not to get close to the flame, even when we want a better view. Mia watches from the marked line and sketches the shape without leaning over the table. At the end, the guide must blow out the candle before moving the holder to the display shelf. We wait until he confirms that it is safe, then ask about the handle and the broad base. The visit shows that questions and careful observation can continue without stepping into a risky space.

Our school keeps a small indoor display space open all year round, not only during special fairs. Each month, a different class chooses one project to explain there. Today, we pass around a booklet showing how our bridge model changed during testing. Visitors compare the first sketch with a later photograph and ask why we added another support. Mia explains the test result, then invites them to write questions on cards beside the booklet. Because the space stays available between events, other classes can return and build on the discussion later.

The village library does not close for any season. It welcomes readers through spring, summer, autumn and winter.

Our class is arranging a visit from a local storyteller for the final club meeting of term. Mia offers to ring her up after school with our teacher present. The storyteller answers but cannot check her calendar while she is travelling on a bus. She promises to ring us back when she reaches home and can look at the dates. Meanwhile, we prepare two possible times and list how long the story and questions may take. The later conversation is brief and clear because both sides now have the information needed to choose.

At the final craft club meeting, our group is busy with a poster showing what we learned this term. We find several unfinished notes but cannot remember which picture belongs with each one. Mia says that from now on, each new sketch should have a date and a short explanation. For the old notes, we compare what everyone remembers and mark uncertain details rather than inventing them. Ben makes a simple example card that the next group can copy when its own project begins. Our final poster records both the finished work and a practical habit that will help future work stay clear.
